summary:
Johor is one of Malaysia's thirteen states and stands under the national framework of Malaysia: federal law criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity throughout the country, and the Johor layer adds Sharia offences that reach Muslims alone. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code, in force in Johor, criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, for men and women alike. The provisions cover oral and anal sex, extend to acts that are consensual and private, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens.

Johor's Sharia enactment prohibits cross-dressing and "males posing as females" alongside liwat and musahaqah. These state offences apply only to Muslims, so a non-Muslim visitor falls under the federal Penal Code alone. Penalties under the national Sharia framework reach three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and the enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, leaving the line between compliant and offending presentation to officers on the ground.

In November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. No source in this inventory reports whether those centres have since opened or what powers would compel attendance.

The Johor announcement sits inside a national crackdown that has run since the 2018 election. At least 1,733 people had attended state-run "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, and state-conducted investigations covered seven states and federal territories, among them Kuala Lumpur, Selangor and Penang.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement machinery operates at state level across the country. Every one of the thirteen states and the federal territories maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", and the Sharia codes of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity. The federal territories are the most frequently reported venue for raids, including a male-only sauna in Chow Kit raided on 28 November 2025 with 208 men arrested under section 377B.

Violence against transgender women in Malaysia is lethal and largely unpunished. A trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and reporting on those killings is obstructed by an investigative process in which police mistreatment and impunity go unexamined.

Identity documents are controlled by the Registration Department, which routinely rejects gender-marker changes; a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holding that sex is determined at birth was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but is applied in practice. The only documented successful marker change is historical and Johor-linked: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors; the nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay.
localsOnly:
Sharia offences in Johor bind Muslims alone, and enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department rather than the police. Residents who are Muslim face the cross-dressing and same-sex provisions directly; non-Muslim residents are subject only to the federal Penal Code.

Custodial and institutional alternatives to prison are prescribed by the same Sharia enactments. Sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months and may order cross-dressing and other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states, a period extended to a year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment.

Residents face the conversion-therapy machinery announced by the Johor government in November 2023, within a national total of at least 1,733 people who had attended "rehabilitation programmes" by June 2021. No legal challenge has removed the framework: the High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds rather than substance.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory supplies no Johor-specific arrest, prosecution or detention figures for transgender or gender-nonconforming people; the documented arrest cases, including the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014, are attributed to other states and to the federal territories. Whether Johor's religious department has conducted comparable operations is unresolved here.

Whether the conversion-therapy centres announced by the Johor government in November 2023 have been built, opened, or given enforcement powers is not sourced. The 1,733 figure for "rehabilitation programme" attendance is a national total as of June 2021 with no state-level breakdown, so its Johor share is unresolved.

Entry and visa policy for transgender visitors is not sourced at state level; the inventory records no Johor-specific border rule and no explicit national visa rule turning on gender identity or presentation.
